3.2 Node-wise Parametric Calibration

TS is the classical parametric calibration approach, which adjusts model confidence by scaling logits with a temperature [MATH T>0] T > 0 T>0 before softmax, smoothing outputs without affecting accuracy. The temperature [MATH T] T T controls the smoothness of predicted probabilities: [MATH T=1] T = 1 T=1 uses logits directly, while increasing [MATH T] T T spreads probabilities, improving calibration in overconfident models.

Recent studies extend this by learning node-wise temperatures for each node [MATH i] i i in graph classification ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Hsu et al., 2022 ) . Commonly, node-wise temperature scaling for calibration is conducted by applying an extra GNN layer to learn the node-wise optimal smoothing parameter [MATH T_{i}] T i T_{i} and do the following operation for the logits: [MATH z_{i}^{\prime}=z_{i}/T_{i}.] z i ′ = z i / T i . z_{i}^{\prime}=z_{i}/T_{i}. (4) We should mention that in training the smoothing temperature [MATH T] T T , the loss function is always the negative log-likelihood function, which is categorized to the proper score ( Gruber & Buettner, 2022 ) in the classification task. The famous ECE error can not be utilized as a training objective function for their discontinuity. Moreover, these post-hoc calibration methods are usually trained on the validation set. We follow these training settings in our main context.
4 GETS
4.1 Ensemble Strategy Meets Node-wise Calibration

Ensemble strategies are widely recognized for improving model robustness and calibration by aggregating predictions from multiple models. For example, in the context of ensemble temperature scaling (ETS) ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) , each model learns its own temperature parameter [MATH T_{m}] T m T_{m} to calibrate its predictions. The ensemble strategy combines the calibrated outputs from multiple calibration models, averaging their predictions to produce a more reliable and better-calibrated result. The ensemble weighting is formulated as a weighted sum over temperature-scaled logits ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) : [MATH T(z)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{m}\cdot t_{m}(z)] T ⁡ ( z ) = ∑ m = 1 M w m ⋅ t m ​ ( z ) T(z)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{m}\cdot t_{m}(z) , where [MATH w_{m}] w m w_{m} are non-negative coefficients summing to 1, and [MATH t_{m}(z)] t m ​ ( z ) t_{m}(z) represents the value of temperature of the [MATH m] m m -th model TS model trained on logit [MATH z] z z , with [MATH M] M M being the number of models.

The ensemble inherits the accuracy-preserving properties from its individual components, with the weights [MATH w_{m}] w m w_{m} controlling the contribution of each calibrated prediction. While ETS leverages model diversity to mitigate overconfidence and improve calibration quality, it falls short in handling the intricate structural problems inherent in graph data. Specifically, ETS considers only the temperatures [MATH t_{m}(z)] t m ​ ( z ) t_{m}(z) , logit [MATH z] z z , and bin size [MATH B] B B to optimize the weights, without incorporating graph structural information such as node degrees. Moreover, the learned temperature is a single value uniformly applied across all nodes, which cannot adapt to the node-wise calibration required in graphs.

We propose to learn a node-wise ensemble strategy for the GNN calibration task. To incorporate the different sources of information, we ensemble based on not only the calibration models but also diverse inputs, including logits [MATH z_{i}] z i z_{i} , node feature [MATH \mathbf{x}_{i}] 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} and node degrees [MATH d_{i}] d i d_{i} , as well as their combination as the calibration model inputs. We use [MATH g_{m}] g m g_{m} to represent the [MATH m] m m -th GNN calibration model that outputs the calibrated logits. Due to the monotone-preserving property of TS, the weighted summation of the logits still keeps the invariant accuracy output. For each node [MATH i] i i , the calibrated logits [MATH z_{i}^{\prime}] z i ′ z_{i}^{\prime} are computed as a weighted sum of the outputs from multiple calibration models: [MATH z_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{i,m}\cdot g_{m}(z_{i},\mathbf{x}_{i},d_{i};\theta_{m}),] z i ′ = ∑ m = 1 M w i , m ⋅ g m ​ ( z i , 𝐱 i , d i , θ m ) , z_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{i,m}\cdot g_{m}(z_{i},\mathbf{x}_{i},d_{i};\theta_{m}), (5) where [MATH w_{i,m}\geq 0] w i , m ≥ 0 w_{i,m}\geq 0 are the node-specific ensemble weights for node [MATH i] i i and model [MATH m] m m , satisfying [MATH \sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{i,m}=1] ∑ m = 1 M w i , m = 1 \sum_{m=1}^{M}w_{i,m}=1 . We further point out that in our expert setting, the input of each expert only contains one element in [MATH \mathbf{x}_{i},d_{i},z_{i}] 𝐱 i , d i , z i \mathbf{x}_{i},d_{i},z_{i} . This gives reasonable learning tasks for different experts and rules out the problem arising in concatenating vectors of different input spaces. Each calibration model [MATH g_{m}] g m g_{m} can focus on different aspects of the calibration process by utilizing various combinations of inputs. For example, one model may calibrate based solely on the logits, another may incorporate node features, and another may consider the node degrees. Specifically, [MATH w_{i,m}] w i , m w_{i,m} can therefore be determined by a gating function [MATH G(\cdot)] G ⁡ ( ⋅ ) G(\cdot) that outputs a probability distribution over the calibration models for each node: [MATH [w_{i,1},w_{i,2},\dots,w_{i,M}]=G(\{g(z_{i},\mathbf{x}_{i},d_{i};\theta_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M};\mathbf{W}_{g},\mathbf{W}_{n}),] [ w i , 1 , w i , 2 , … , w i , M ] = G ⁡ ( { g ⁡ ( z i , 𝐱 i , d i , θ m ) } m = 1 M , 𝐖 g , 𝐖 n ) , [w_{i,1},w_{i,2},\dots,w_{i,M}]=G(\{g(z_{i},\mathbf{x}_{i},d_{i};\theta_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M};\mathbf{W}_{g},\mathbf{W}_{n}), (6) where [MATH \mathbf{W}_{g}] 𝐖 g \mathbf{W}_{g} and [MATH \mathbf{W}_{n}] 𝐖 n \mathbf{W}_{n} represent the parameters of the gating function [MATH G(\cdot)] G ⁡ ( ⋅ ) G(\cdot) , which will be introduced later on. We ensemble the feature inputs by concatenating different combinations of inputs into [MATH g_{m}(\cdot)] g m ​ ( ⋅ ) g_{m}(\cdot) . The key component that remains unknown is how we should do the information aggregation and obtain the gating function to select models.

We include logits [MATH z] z z , node features [MATH \mathbf{x}] 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , and degree (embeddings) [MATH d] d d to capture key factors influencing calibration. Including logits is crucial because they contain the raw prediction information before applying softmax, reflecting the model’s confidence. Incorporating node features allows the model to address individual calibration needs, as feature-based methods binning methods have successfully captured unique sample point characteristics in calibration task ( Huang et al., 2022 ) . Adding degree embeddings tackles structural disparities since our experiments show that degree imbalance leads to varying calibration errors among nodes. Note that degrees are the foundation for graph structure information but we also explore other structural features as inputs in Appendix A.9 . By combining these inputs, our ensemble leverages multiple information sources, resulting in a more robust and effective calibration strategy.
4.2 Ensemble Calibration by Graph MoE

The node-wise ensemble idea mentioned in the last section coincides with the so-called MoE framework ( Jordan & Jacobs, 1994 ; Jacobs et al., 1991 ; Jacobs, 1995 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . MoE allows for specialization by assigning different experts to handle distinct inputs, enabling each expert to focus on specific factors. This specialization is particularly beneficial when inputs are diverse, as it allows experts to learn the unique properties of each factor more effectively than one single GAT model ( Hsu et al., 2022 ) for many inputs at the same time. Moreover, MoE employs sparse activation through a gating network, which selectively activates only relevant experts for each input, reducing computational overhead compared to the dense computation in GATs ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Lepikhin et al., 2020 ) . The overall framework design is shown in Figure 2 ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) . To adapt MoE for graph-based calibration tasks, we propose the GETS framework that integrates both the input ensemble and the model ensembles. In GNNs like GCNs, nodes update their representations by aggregating information from their neighbors. The standard GCN propagation rule is ( Wang et al., 2024 ) : [MATH \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime}=\sigma\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{|d_{i}||d_{j}|}}\mathbf{h}_{j}\mathbf{W}\right),] 𝐡 i ′ = σ ⁡ ( ∑ j ∈ 𝒩 i 1 | d i | ​ | d j | ​ 𝐡 j ​ 𝐖 ) , \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime}=\sigma\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{|d_{i}||d_{j}|}}\mathbf{h}_{j}\mathbf{W}\right), (7) where [MATH \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime}] 𝐡 i ′ \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime} is the updated feature vector for node [MATH i] i i after the GCN layer, [MATH d_{i}] d i d_{i} is the set of neighboring nodes of node [MATH i] i i . We train different GCNs based on various ensemble of inputs as different experts, [MATH \mathbf{d}_{j}] 𝐝 j \mathbf{d}_{j} is the feature vector of the neighboring node [MATH j] j j , and [MATH \mathbf{W}] 𝐖 \mathbf{W} is a learnable matrix for the GCN network. [MATH \frac{1}{\sqrt{|d_{i}||d_{j}|}}] 1 | d i | ​ | d j | \frac{1}{\sqrt{|d_{i}||d_{j}|}} is the normalization term where [MATH |d_{i}|] | d i | |d_{i}| and [MATH |d_{j}|] | d j | |d_{j}| are the degrees (number of neighbors) of nodes [MATH i] i i and [MATH j] j j , respectively. In many GNN papers, the normalization term is also denoted by [MATH \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}] 𝐃 ~ − 1 / 2 𝐀 ~ 𝐃 ~ − 1 / 2 \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} with [MATH \tilde{\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{I}] 𝐀 ~ = 𝐀 + 𝐈 \tilde{\mathbf{A}}=\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{I} is the adjacency matrix with added self-loops. [MATH \tilde{\mathbf{D}}] 𝐃 ~ \tilde{\mathbf{D}} is the corresponding degree matrix with [MATH \tilde{\mathbf{D}}_{ii}=\sum_{j}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{ij}] 𝐃 ~ i ​ i = ∑ j 𝐀 ~ i ​ j \tilde{\mathbf{D}}_{ii}=\sum_{j}\tilde{\mathbf{A}}_{ij} and [MATH \sigma] σ \sigma is a non-linear activation function.

Following our aforementioned notations, the Graph MoE framework introduces multiple experts by learning different GNN models with a gating mechanism for aggregation. The propagation rule in Graph MoE training is: [MATH \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime}=\sigma\left(\sum_{m=1}^{M}G(\mathbf{h}_{i})_{m}\cdot g_{m}\left(\mathbf{h}_{j};\theta_{m}\right)\right),] 𝐡 i ′ = σ ⁡ ( ∑ m = 1 M G ​ ( 𝐡 i ) m ⋅ g m ​ ( 𝐡 j , θ m ) ) , \mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime}=\sigma\left(\sum_{m=1}^{M}G(\mathbf{h}_{i})_{m}\cdot g_{m}\left(\mathbf{h}_{j};\theta_{m}\right)\right), (8)

where, for consistency with Equation 5 , [MATH g_{m}(\cdot)] g m ​ ( ⋅ ) g_{m}(\cdot) represents the [MATH m] m m -th GNN expert function that processes a specific ensemble of inputs—such as logits [MATH z_{i}] z i z_{i} , node features [MATH \mathbf{x}_{i}] 𝐱 i \mathbf{x}_{i} , and node degrees. The model is trained by minimizing a calibration loss over all nodes: [MATH L=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{\text{cal}}\left(z_{i}^{\prime},y_{i}\right)] L = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ℓ cal ​ ( z i ′ , y i ) L=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{\text{cal}}\left(z_{i}^{\prime},y_{i}\right) , where [MATH \ell_{\text{cal}}] ℓ cal \ell_{\text{cal}} is a differentiable calibration loss function (e.g., cross-entropy loss) mentioned before and [MATH N] N N is the number of nodes. The backbone GNN models used for calibration are identical to the base classification models, ensuring consistent feature extraction and processing. We tune the hidden dimension for the calibrators from the set [MATH \{16,32,64\}] { 16 , 32 , 64 } \{16,32,64\} , depending on the dataset’s complexity, while dropout rates are chosen between 0.2 and 0.8 to balance regularization and model performance.

GETS includes an expert selection mechanism that incorporates logits, features, and node degree information, either individually or in combination, depending on the configuration that best fits the dataset. For all experiments, we maintain a fixed bin size of 10 for uncertainty estimation. The calibrators are trained with a learning rate of either [MATH 1\times 10^{-1}] 1 × 10 − 1 1\times 10^{-1} or [MATH 1\times 10^{-3}] 1 × 10 − 3 1\times 10^{-3} , depending on the model’s complexity, and we tune weight decay ranging from [MATH 0] 0 0 to [MATH 0.1] 0.1 0.1 to regularize the training process further. The calibrators are trained for up to 1000 epochs, with early stopping applied based on patience of 50 epochs.
